Your job search, on your own server: one profile, a tailored resume and cover letter for every job, and every application tracked from draft to offer.

It's for one person on a small server: one password, your data in your own PostgreSQL database, and an AI model of your choice. That can be a local model through Ollama or LM Studio, so your profile and documents stay on your own hardware, or a hosted one (any OpenAI-compatible API, Anthropic or Mistral), which then receives what it writes from. Privacy says what goes where.

**Get started:** run it on your computer in a few minutes, or self-host it on a server. The installation guide covers every way: Docker with or without Compose, Node.js, a plain Ubuntu server, CapRover, Coolify and Dokploy.

All you need is Docker Desktop on macOS or Windows, or Docker Engine with its Compose plugin on Linux, and about 2 GB of free memory. Run the commands in a terminal: macOS's Terminal, Linux, or WSL on Windows.

On an Apple Silicon Mac, also run `printf 'services:
 app:
 platform: linux/amd64
' > compose.override.yml`: the image is built for Intel and AMD processors, and Docker Desktop runs it under emulation.

The first start downloads the image (about 1.7 GB) and sets up the database. Open http://localhost:3000, sign in with your password, and pick an AI model in **Settings → AI provider** (see Choosing an AI provider).

`docker compose stop` stops it and `docker compose start` starts it again, with your data kept. It's only reachable from your own computer. The installation guide's Docker Compose page has more: another port, your time zone, upgrades and removing it.

To put Dossier on a server, on your own domain with HTTPS, follow the installation guide: a plain Ubuntu server with Docker Compose and Caddy (or Node.js, without Docker), CapRover, Coolify or Dokploy. Give the server at least 2 vCPUs and 2 GB of memory (see Performance and sizing).
The wiki has what comes after installing:
- Choosing an AI provider: a hosted model, or a local one with Ollama or LM Studio.
- Choosing a job source: JSearch, Adzuna or FreeHire (and an unofficial one for Germany), and the job agent.
- Connecting Gmail and Calendar: your own Google OAuth client, step by step.
- Connecting Claude: the MCP connector, in Claude's apps and on the command line.
- Backups and restore: exports, nightly backups and database dumps.
- Troubleshooting: what the common errors mean, and what to do about them.
- Privacy: what stays on your server and what leaves it. PRIVACY.md has the details.
- Environment variables: every setting the server reads.
What protects your data, how to run Dossier safely and how to report a problem: see SECURITY.md.
Working on Dossier itself: see DEVELOPMENT.md.

|**Model products and pricing**|Define versioned plans, features, add-ons, and flat, recurring, per-unit, tiered, package, or dynamic prices; then assign customer subscriptions.|
|**Control access**|Calculate feature access and usage-limit balances for your application to enforce, with one-time or recurring entitlement grants.|
|**Bill usage**|Rate flat and usage-based charges, manage customer credit balances and subscription changes, and run the invoice lifecycle.|
|**Integrate**|Use the OSS REST API and JavaScript, Python, or Go SDKs, send webhooks, and connect external invoicing providers.|

A complete SQL (and also non-SQL) databases of Vietnamese administrative units, includes all **34 Vietnamese provinces** and associated districts, wards sub-divisions.
Data is updated as of the most recent effective decree: [388/NQ-UBTVQH16][source government decree]
The author(s) of this repository is not associated with the **General Statistics Office of Vietnam**, nor the Vietnamese government.
The data of provinces and wards are created base on the [API province data provided by the General Statistics Office of Vietnam website][source goverment API].
This dataset also include additional information apart from the original provinces, wards data from the original data. Please see section Additional change make by this repository.
The Vietnamese Government may issue decree from time to time to adjust the administrative unit structure. You can track the latest issued decrees [here][decree issued page].
- Assigned administrative units to province and ward data
- Generated English names for provinces and wards, offering both full and short forms
- Generated code names (slugs) for provinces and wards
The `provinces` table contains a list of **first administrative tier - the provincial level** units, includes **34** municipalities and provinces.
|`code`|varchar(20)|The official unit code, defined by government|Primary Key|
|`administrative_unit_id`|integer|The administrative unit id of this record|Foreign Key, references to `administrative_units.id`|
The `wards` table contains a list of **second administrative tier - the commune level** units, includes **3321** wards, communes and special administrative region.
|`code`|varchar(20)|The official unit code, defined by government|Primary Key|
|`administrative_unit_id`|integer|The administrative unit id of this record|Foreign Key, references to `administrative_units.id`|
You can easily create query to get all the kind of data you need since the tables are clearly referenced between each others.
In addition to the administrative units dataset, this repository also includes optional add-on data extend its functionality.

`pg_easy_replicate` is a CLI orchestrator tool that simplifies the process of setting up logical replication between two PostgreSQL databases. `pg_easy_replicate` also supports switchover. After the source (primary database) is fully replicated, `pg_easy_replicate` puts it into read-only mode and via logical replication flushes all data to the new target database. This ensures zero data loss and minimal downtime for the application. This method can be useful for performing minimal downtime (up to <1min, depending) major version upgrades between a Blue/Green PostgreSQL database setup, load testing and other similar use cases.

In this strategy, you have a weighted based DNS system (example AWS Route53 weighted records) where 100% of traffic goes to a primary origin and 0% to a secondary origin. The primary origin here is the DNS host for your source database and secondary origin is the DNS host for your target database. You can set up your application ahead of time to interact with the database using DNS from the weighted group.
